ERSSTv6 is a global monthly analysis of sea surface temperatures, extending from January 1850 to the present, on a 2° x 2° latitude-longitude grid. Details: Australian Climate Influences About these graphs Climate indices An index is a measure (often a numerical value) that can be representative of a particular pattern or state of a system. Climatologists monitor several indices, some ocean-based and some atmospheric, to provide a quick indication of the state of certain climate variables and climate indicators. El Ni o–Southern Oscillation indices El Ni o and La Ni a (collectively referred to as the El Ni o–Southern Oscillation or ENSO) are characterised by changes in the equatorial Pacific Ocean. During El Ni o, sea surface temperatures (SST) in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become warmer than average, while during La Ni a these SSTs become cooler than average. Niño indices regions To monitor the Pacific Ocean for signs of El Niño or La Niña, climatologists use several SST indices. These indices measure the difference between the current sea surface temperature and its long-term (1991–2020) average in several regions located along the equatorial Pacific. The difference is referred to as an anomaly. These regions are labelled Niño1, Niño2, Niño3, Niño3.4 and Niño4 and are used by meteorological agencies around the world. Relative Niño indices Traditional Niño index values were used at the Bureau of Meteorology until September 2025. From September 2025, the Bureau has used Relative Niño indices, which measure sea surface temperature anomalies in the tropical Pacific Ocean in the Niño regions, but calculated relative to the global tropical region temperature anomaly. The SOI is calculated using the pressure differences between Tahiti and Darwin. Sustained negative values of the SOI below −7 often indicate El Niño is active while sustained positive values above +7 are typical of a La Niña. Further Information on ENSO ENSO conditions are monitored by analysing Pacific sea surface temperatures (SSTs), low level winds, cloudiness (using outgoing longwave radiation), and subsurface temperatures. Special attention is given to SSTs, as they are one of the key indicators used to monitor ENSO. Here, three different datasets are used: HadISST1.1, ERSSTv5, and COBE2 datasets. The Relative Nino3.4 index is used, which compares the SSTs in the Nino3.4 region with the tropical average, accounting for long-term and other shifts in the climate. El Niño (La Niña) conditions are associated with warmer (colder) SST anomalies in the central and eastern Pacific. The threshold for an El Niño (La Niña) in the Nino3.4 Region is above 0.6°C (below -0.6°C). El Niño (La Niña) conditions also correspond to an increase (decrease) in cloudiness around or to the east of the international dateline (180°), with a decrease (increase) in cloudiness in the west. There is also a decrease (increase) in the trade winds in the eastern Pacific. Sub-surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific should also be warmer (colder) than average, to sustain the El Niño (La Niña) conditions. International climate centres use different criteria, including different SST thresholds, suitable for their own region and applications. Therefore, variations between centres on the current ENSO state should be expected, especially when conditions are borderline. The relative sea surface temperatures (SSTs) in the tropical Pacific in October 2026 were above average in the central and eastern portion of the region and below-average in the west (Figure 1). The warm (positive) anomalies in the Nino3.4 region (red box) are indicative of the El Niño conditions during October 2026. SSTs were below average over the eastern equatorial Indian ocean and near-to above average over the western equatorial Indian ocean, resulting in a positive Indian Ocean Dipole index and, along with atmospheric and oceanic indicators (not shown), support the presence of positive IOD conditions. Figure 1: Relative SST anomalies (to the average tropical SST anomaly) for October 2026 using ERSST v5 data. Red (blue) shades show regions of relative warming (cooling). The tropical Pacific Ocean Nino3.4 Region is outlined in red. The Indian Ocean Dipole index is the difference between average SST anomalies over the western Indian Ocean (black solid box) and the eastern Indian Ocean (black dotted box). Looking at the Relative Nino3.4 index in Figure 2, the 1-month Relative Nino3.4 index was negative, but within the neutral range, until August 2025. The index passed the La Niña threshold in September 2025 and returned to the neutral range in March 2026. Since then, the index has continued to warm. The May 2026 value was just below the El Niño threshold, with the June 2026 value passing the El Niño threshold and further warming continuing through to October 2026. For El Niño conditions to be present, 1-month warm SST anomalies (observed or forecast) should persist for at least four months above the El Niño threshold, with at least one of the months observed; along with supporting atmospheric observations. Figure 2: The Nino3.4 index using the 1-month SST anomalies. Warm anomalies (≥ +0.65; brown) correspond to El Niño conditions while cold anomalies (≤ -0.65; blue) correspond to La Niña conditions; otherwise neutral ( -0.65 and +0.65; grey). Model outlooks from Copernicus C3S (Figure 3), based on the Relative Nino3.4 SST index, predict the El Niño conditions to continue strengthening until November – December 2026. Most models predict the El Niño conditions to begin to weaken in January – February 2027, with some models predicting a rapid decay while others predict a more gradual decay. Most models (> 70%) predict El Niño conditions will still be present in April 2027. The blue and yellow lines note the La Niña and El Niño thresholds, respectively, used by various centres. Historical ENSO Variability To classify a historical El Niño event, the 3-month average Nino3.4 value must be above 0.65°C for 5 or more consecutive months. For La Niña events, the threshold is -0.65°C. Otherwise it is considered neutral. ENSO events with a peak value above 1.5°C (El Niño) or below -1.5°C (La Niña) are considered strong. Otherwise, the events are considered weak to moderate in strength. The following figure (Figure 4) shows the development of the Nino3.4 index for the most recent El Niño and La Niña events in comparison to other El Niño/La Niña events. Figure 4: Three-month Nino3.4 index development and retreat of different El Niño (left)/La Niña (right) events since the 1960s. Recent El Niño and La Niña events are in red and purple, respectively. Impact of El Niño/La Niña on Southeast Asia The typical impact of El Niño on the Southeast Asia region is drier-than-average rainfall conditions, including for most of the Maritime Continent during December – February (Figure 5a), and warmer temperatures. The opposite conditions for rainfall are observed during La Niña years (Figure 5b). The impact on the region’s rainfall and temperature from ENSO events is more significantly felt during strong- or moderate-intensity events. Also, no two El Niño events or two La Niña events are exactly alike in terms of their impact on the region. In South East Asia, this brings drier weather and increases the risk of forest fires and smoke haze. The La Niña phenomenon is the reverse of the El Niño where cooler waters develop over the Eastern Tropical Pacific Ocean along the coast of South America. In South East Asia, higher than normal rainfall tends to occur during a La Niña episode which may result in an increased occurrence of floods. These are expected to strengthen further through end-2026, with Monsoon Mission Coupled Forecast System (MMCFS) indicating a high likelihood of strong-to-very strong El Niño conditions persisting through January–March 2027. Currently, neutral IOD conditions prevail over the Indian Ocean. Sea surface temperatures are warmer than normal in both the western and eastern equatorial Indian Ocean, with stronger warming in the west. MMCFS predicts that neutral IOD conditions are most likely to continue throughout the forecast period, while some international centres expect the positive IOD phase to continue in the near term. 1. Current Sea Surface Temperature (SST) Conditions over the Pacific and Indian Oceans During September 2026, El Niño conditions strengthened further relative to August. SST anomalies exceeded +2.0°C over the eastern equatorial Pacific, with positive anomalies intensifying east of the Date Line and extending across the eastern basin (Fig. 1a). Aboveaverage SSTs were also observed over parts of the North Pacific and several other global ocean regions, while near-normal to slightly below-normal SSTs prevailed over portions of the southern Pacific and south Atlantic. Compared with August 2026, positive SST anomalies strengthened over the eastern equatorial Pacific, whereas cooling occurred over parts of the central and western equatorial Pacific as well as parts of the northern and southern subtropical Pacific (Fig. 1b). In September 2026, positive SST anomalies were observed over both the western and eastern Indian Ocean (Fig. 1a). Compared with August 2026, warm SST anomalies strengthened over the western and central equatorial Indian Ocean, while cooling occurred over the eastern equatorial Indian Ocean and the Bay of Bengal. The Arabian Sea continued to exhibit warm SSTs (Fig. 1b). 1 1.1 El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) conditions over the Pacific Ocean The monthly time series of Niño 3.4 SST anomalies for the 12-month period from October 2025 to September 2026 is shown in Fig. 2a. La Niña conditions persisted from September 2025 through February 2026 and transitioned to ENSO-neutral conditions in March 2026. Subsequently, the Niño 3.4 SST anomalies increased rapidly, crossing the El Niño threshold in May 2026 and strengthening further to approximately +2.0°C by September 2026, indicating the strong El Niño conditions over the central equatorial Pacific Ocean. Strong positive subsurface temperature anomalies are observed across much of the eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean both near and above the 20°C isotherm, extending down to the thermocline. Negative SST anomalies were observed over the western and central equatorial Pacific, with the strongest negative anomalies in the central equatorial Pacific (Fig. 2b). 1.2. Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) conditions over the Indian Ocean Fig. 2c shows the monthly variation of the Dipole Mode Index (DMI) over the Indian Ocean from October 2025 to September 2026. Negative IOD conditions persisted from October to December 2025, followed by a gradual weakening of the negative phase. The DMI remained near neutral in January 2026 and turned positive during February–April 2026, indicating relatively warmer SSTs over the western equatorial Indian Ocean compared to the eastern equatorial Indian Ocean. Thereafter, the DMI gradually turned to negative during May–June 2026. Neutral IOD conditions prevailed from July to August 2026. Both western and eastern equatorial boxes show positive SST anomalies, with the west warmer with DMI index 0.6°C. However, currently neutral IOD conditions prevail over the Indian Ocean. Positive subsurface temperature anomalies (Fig. 2d) are observed in the western and central equatorial Indian Ocean below the 20°C isotherm, extending down to the thermocline. Negative SST anomalies were observed over the eastern Indian Ocean. Probability density function (PDF)-based bias correction was applied to the forecasts of the Niño 3.4 index (Fig. 4a&4b) and the Dipole Mode Index (DMI); Fig. 5a&5b) using hindcasts for the period 1999–2008. Forecast anomalies were computed relative to the 1991–2020 climatological mean. The three-month seasonally averaged SST anomaly forecast over the Pacific Ocean (Fig. 3) indicates that positive anomalies are likely to strengthen over the central equatorial Pacific during October–December (OND) 2026. From November–January (NDJ) 2026–27 onwards, these positive anomalies are expected to intensify further and expand across both the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. Over the Indian Ocean, the same forecast suggests that near-neutral SST anomalies are likely to prevail across most regions during the upcoming seasons (Fig. 3). The latest MMCFS plume and probability forecasts (Figs. 4a and 4b) indicate that strong to very strong El Niño conditions are likely to persist during the upcoming season. IMD will continue to closely monitor the evolving ENSO conditions and issue monthly updates based on the latest observations from the Pacific Ocean. Currently, neutral Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) conditions prevail over the Indian Ocean, as the required threshold for establishing an IOD event has not been sustained. Operational forecasting capacity is also being strengthened through the Severe Weather Forecasting Programme (SWFP)-Caribbean. During the June 2026 Operational Testbed Workshop in Barbados, forecasters from across the region participated in simulations, case studies and operational exercises. The workshop also established an operational coordination mechanism linking forecasting centres and national focal points, creating a stronger framework for coordinated action during severe weather events. The region continues to promote preparedness through broader stakeholder engagement. Youth awareness initiatives gained international recognition through the Caribbean Lightning Safety Awareness Contest, which was highlighted in the COPE Disaster Champions publication as an example of disaster preparedness education for children. Together, these initiatives are helping Caribbean countries transform regional climate and weather information into coordinated national action before hazards materialize. Enhancing water security and early warnings across Pacific island states Pacific Small Island Developing States (SIDS) are highly vulnerable to El Niño impacts, particularly prolonged drought, water shortages and disruptions to agriculture and livelihoods. Through the Scale Up Inclusive Early Warning and Action in the Pacific (CREWS SIEWAP) project and the Drought Resilience and Early Warning (DREW) Pacific project, WMO is supporting various countries and territories in the Pacific to strengthen preparedness and resilience. National Climate Outlook Forum (NCOF) support has been provided for Papua New Guinea and Tokelau, enabling them to interpret seasonal forecasts and develop context-specific preparedness measures ahead of expected climate impacts. The project are also supporting the development of Drought Management Plans across participating countries, helping establish structured approaches for drought preparedness, monitoring and response. Regional collaboration remains a cornerstone of implementation. Support to the Pacific Islands Climate Outlook Forum (PICOF), the Samoa Groundwater Strategy and community-based early warning activities in the Federated States of Micronesia are helping strengthen climate services and water security across the region. In Vanuatu, community-level resilience measures are demonstrating tangible results. High-resolution impact data collection has been completed across Epi, Ambae and Santo islands, public awareness materials have been produced, peer-review arrangements established and community-based water tank projects implemented ahead of schedule. These interventions help communities better understand local climate risks while improving access to water during drought periods associated with El Niño conditions. Turning warnings into early action The global El Niño response highlights the importance of connecting climate science with practical implementation. From strengthening national meteorological services in Cabo Verde, to drought planning in Southeast Asia, operational forecasting in the Caribbean and water resilience initiatives across the Pacific, WMO projects are helping countries ensure that authoritative climate information reaches those who need it most. NMHSs are critical to El Niño preparedness and response. As the authoritative source of weather, climate and water information, NMHSs provide the forecasts, warnings, and climate services that enable governments, humanitarian organizations, businesses, and communities to act ahead of hazardous events. However, forecasts alone do not save lives. Effective preparedness requires NMHSs to work closely with disaster management authorities, sectoral ministries, humanitarian partners, the private sector and local communities to translate climate science into informed decisions and early action. This collaborative approach lies at the core of the Early Warnings for All (EW4All) initiative. EW4All brings together the diverse investments, partnerships, programmes and technical efforts needed across the entire MHEWS value chain, from risk knowledge, observations and forecasting, to warning dissemination, preparedness and early action. El Niño preparedness and response has been bolstered thanks to the progress on EW4All. Share: Related Topics El Niño / La Niña Phenomena Related Projects Strengthening Hydro-Meteorological and Multi-Hazard Early Warning Services in the Caribbean - Phase 2 (CREWS Caribbean 2.0) Scale up Inclusive Early Warning and Action in the Pacific (CREWS SIEWAP) Strengthening early warning and early action systems for meteorological, hydrological and climate extremes in Cambodia and Lao People’s Democratic Republic (PDR) (CREWS Cambodia and Lao PDR 2.0) Drought Resilience and Early Warning (DREW) Pacific Project El Niño and La Niña are opposite phases of a naturally occurring climate pattern known as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), involving fluctuating ocean temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, coupled with changes in the overlying atmosphere. Specifically, El Niño is characterized by unusually warm ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific. WMO has stepped up support across its 194 Members in response to El Niño. WMO quarterly El Niño/La Niña Updates and monthly Global Seasonal Climate Updates guide early action by tracking El Niño and other climate drivers. Regional Climate Outlook Forums help national weather and water services tailor forecasts for decisionmakers, while the WMO Coordination Mechanism provides expert advice for humanitarian preparedness and early action. WMO projects are a critical part of the El Niño efforts. Projects allow for implementation at the regional and national levels, enabling authoritative warnings and advisories to be shared in a timely manner to enable informed decision-making and action. Across Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and the Pacific regions, WMO-supported initiatives have been providing operational, technical, and institutional support to enhance preparedness and early action. The following is a scan across the regions on what WMO projects are accomplishing in the context of El Niño. Strengthening national institutional resilience in Cabo Verde In Cabo Verde, WMO support is strengthening Cabo Verde’s preparedness for, and response to, El Niño by enhancing the country’s capacity to produce, share and use timely weather and climate information. Support to Cabo Verde’s National Institute of Meteorology and Geophysics (INMG) includes launching its new website, improving data exchange, facilitating access to global forecasting products, and disseminating forecasts and alerts in Common Alerting Protocol (CAP) format. These improvements strengthen the national multi-hazard early warning system (MHEWS) and provide decisionmakers with more timely, accessible and actionable information for El Niño preparedness and response. Through the CREWS Accelerated Support Window Cabo Verde project , the country developed and validated a national MHEWS roadmap with time-bound actions to deliver early warnings for all. This has been supported by two national resolutions, one establishing the MHEWS national coordination mechanism and the other rolling out the implementation of the MHEWS national roadmap. The project is also strengthening the institutional foundations needed for sustainable MHEWS delivery. This includes developing INMG’s new National Strategic Plan, Human Resources Plan and Capacity Improvement Plan, as well as exploring a socio-economic assessment to demonstrate the value of its services, advocate for increased resources and raise the institution’s visibility. Beyond INMG, the project is helping secure high-level political support for MHEWS and enabling the development and validation of a national Early Warnings for All roadmap. By bringing together relevant ministries and sectors, the roadmap will establish a coordinated, whole-of-government approach to strengthening MHEWS, including preparedness for and response to El Niño and other climate-related hazards. Strengthening drought preparedness and water resilience in Cambodia & Lao PDR In Southeast Asia, WMO-supported activities are helping Cambodia and Lao PDR strengthen resilience to one of the most common consequences of El Niño: drought. Through the CREWS-funded project , both countries are developing National Integrated Water Resources Management Plans and National Action Plans on Drought Management and Adaptation for 2025-2030. These initiatives seek to integrate water management, land-use planning and climate information into coherent national strategies that support sustainable water resource management and climate resilience. The drought action plans are designed to strengthen national capacity to assess, manage and reduce drought risks while improving long-term adaptation to increasingly variable climate conditions. By providing structured frameworks for decision-making, these plans support sectors such as agriculture, water supply and rural development that are particularly vulnerable to El Niño-related rainfall deficits. Seasonal Monsoon Forums supported in both countries further strengthen preparedness. The wet-season forum was held in May 2026, while a dry-season forum is scheduled for November 2026, providing opportunities for forecasters, decisionmakers and sectoral users to examine seasonal outlooks and plan accordingly. Advancing multi-hazard early warning systems in the Caribbean The Caribbean region faces a complex mix of hydro-meteorological hazards that can be influenced by El Niño, including drought, heat stress, wildfire risk and changes in tropical cyclone activity. Through the CREWS Caribbean 2.0 project and related regional initiatives, WMO is helping countries improve forecasting capabilities, warning dissemination and regional coordination. A major milestone is the regional workshop on Impact-Based Forecast and Warning Services (IBFWS) and the Common Alerting Protocol, held in Trinidad and Tobago in May 2026. The workshop brought together NMHSs, disaster management agencies and other stakeholders to strengthen practical application of impact-based forecasting and warning dissemination. Particular emphasis was placed on improving communication to vulnerable and last-mile communities. The Himalayan glacier collapse and catastrophic downstream flash flood in late August killed more than 1,300 people and had a massive impact on Nepal’s economy. Tropical cyclones caused devastation and loss of life in many countries. The current El Niño is expected to act as a risk multiplier for health. Increased heat, drought and heavy rainfall can contribute to heat-related illness and mortality, wildfire smoke and poor air quality, malnutrition and food insecurity, injuries, and changing risks of water- and vector-borne diseases such as cholera, malaria and dengue. The World Health Organization (WHO) has, for the first time, classified the anticipated health impacts as a health emergency. El Niño is already increasing risks for agriculture in key seasons and production systems, especially in areas where there is high food insecurity and heavy reliance on rainfed agriculture. It highlights the knock-on risks to the environment, economy, and everyday life. Key messages 2026 will be one of four warmest years on record El Niño turns up the heat and multiplies risks Sea level and ocean heat are at record high levels Extreme weather has massive economic and human cost Forecasts and warnings, underpinned by sustained observations, are vital Share: WMO 2027 Calendar Competition - Gaël Handschin The WMO State of the Climate Update 2026 shows that the past 12 years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years being the top four. The global average surface temperature for January–September 2026 was about 1.47 °Celsius above the pre-industrial average. This figure is likely to rise through the end of the year because of the warming effect of El Niño, which has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December. Earth’s energy imbalance is rising and the earth system is accumulating heat at an accelerating rate. The imbalance reached its highest level since monitoring began, as greenhouse gases trap unprecedented amounts of heat and upset the equilibrium between incoming energy from the sun and outgoing energy. The ocean absorbs 90% of this excess heat and 2026 is on track to be the tenth successive year of record ocean warmth. Sea level is the highest on record, and sea-surface temperatures hit monthly records during 2026. The long-term retreat of glaciers continues - the annual mass loss of ice in 2025 would have filled five Olympic pools every second of the year. Freshwater storage has been dwindling since 2014. “We have entered a new age of climate extremes. A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst. Leaders must get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need.” said UN Secretary-General António Guterres. “ El Niño and indeed the state of the global climate in 2026 gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts. El Niño doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat from the ocean, which is the warmest ever measured. There is simply more heat available to release,” said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo . “We are supercharging our weather and El Niño will be a risk multiplier. Heatwaves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for. Hundreds of millions of people this year have been exposed to unbearable extreme heat, whilst the catastrophic ice and rock collapse and flash floods in Nepal highlighted the compound risks facing communities in fragile, warming high-mountain terrain.” Forecasts underpinned by sustained observations from every part of the world are more important than ever to monitor our rapidly changing climate and help navigate the increasing risks to societies and economies. The good news is that the number of countries reporting the existence of multi-hazard early warning systems (MHEWSs) has increased from 56 in 2015 to 136 in 2025, according to the report. The WMO State of the Climate 2026 Update was released on the first day of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, as an authoritative, science-based report. It includes data – where available – up to September 2026 and therefore does not reflect the most recent impacts of El Niño. The final State of the Global Climate 2026 report will be issued in March 2027, incorporating scientific contributions from dozens of National Meteorological and Hydrological Services, regional climate centres, United Nations partners and experts from the WMO community. Highlights Global temperature: The global mean near-surface temperature anomaly averaged from January to September 2026 (1.47 °C ± 0.13 °C above the 1850–1900 average) is comparable to the whole-year averages for 2025 (1.43 °C) and 2023 (1.46 °C) and lower than the 2024 record (1.55 °C). This is based on nine internationally recognized datasets. The past four years, 2023-2026, are the four warmest years on record. La Niña conditions at the start of the year had a temporary cooling effect, which was reversed by the development of El Niño. Global monthly average sea-surface temperatures were the highest or second highest on record for June, July and August, and monthly global temperatures were among the three highest for the time of year from May to September. El Niño is forecast to continue into early 2027. El Niño typically boosts annual global mean temperatures by around 0.1 °C–0.2 °C, and it is likely that the final anomaly for 2026 will be higher than the January to September average. El Niño typically has the greatest impact on global average temperatures in the year after its development. Greenhouse gas levels reached a new record in 2025. Atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide has increased by 53% from around 278 parts per million (ppm) in 1750 to about 426.8 ppm in 2025. Global averaged methane concentrations increased from 729 parts per billion (ppb) in 1750 by 167% to 1 948 ppb in 2025. Nitrous oxide concentrations increased by 26% from 270 ppb in 1750 to 339.1 ppb in 2025. Measurements from benchmark monitoring stations (such as Mauna Loa in Hawaii and Kennaook/Cape Grim in Australia), indicate a continued increase in 2026. El Niño events typically lead to a surge in greenhouse gas concentrations. Earth’s energy imbalance: Ocean heat measurements and satellite observations show an acceleration in the rate at which the Earth system is accumulating heat. In 2025, it reached its highest observed value since monitoring began in 1960. Preliminary values for January–July 2026 suggest another record high. Ocean heat content in the upper 2 000 meters was the highest in the observed record in 2025 and has continued to rise in 2026, according to preliminary data (to July). Ocean warming rates have accelerated with a particularly strong increase over the past two decades, impacting marine ecosystems, biodiversity, and the ocean’s role as a carbon sink. Ocean heat intensifies tropical and subtropical storms, accelerates sea-ice loss in the polar regions, and – together with melting land ice – drives sea-level rise. This warming is projected to continue for hundreds to thousands of years. Global mean sea level reached a record high in 2026. Sea-level rise has accelerated since the start of the satellite record as a result of increased melting of glaciers and ice sheets, as well as increased thermal expansion of warming waters. June, July and August 2026 saw their highest values since the beginning of the satellite altimetry era in 1993. This sharp increase may reflect changes associated with the developing El Niño, including a shift in rainfall from land to ocean in the western tropical Pacific. Sea ice: In 2026, Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest annual maximum on record (in the satellite era since 1979), while the Arctic maximum was the lowest or second lowest. around: Ministry of Labour & Employment Centre Writes to Chief Secretaries/Administrators of all States/UTs on Measures for Effective Management and mitigation of Adverse Effects of Extreme Heat Waves on Workers and Labourers Posted On: 22 APR 2025 5:02PM by PIB Delhi The Ministry of Labour and Employment has advised all States and UTs to ensure effective measures to reduce the impact of extreme heat waves on workers and labourers engaged in different sectors. In a letter addressed to Chief Secretaries /Administrators of all States/UTs, Secretary, Ministry of of Labour & Employment emphasized upon the need to issue directions to the occupiers / employers / construction companies / industries to undertake necessary steps to mitigate the adverse effects of extreme heatwave on workers/labourers. The letter recommended for a coordinated, multi-sectoral approach listing out various steps including rescheduling of working hours, ensuring adequate drinking water facilities, ventilation and cooling of work places, rest areas, conducting regular health check-ups for workers and providing emergency ice packs and heat illness prevention materials to construction workers etc. The letter also advised for instructions to be issued to mine and factory managements to allow slower work pace, flexible schedules, two-person crews during extreme heat, proper ventilation in underground mines. In addition to factories and mines, it stressed upon special attention to be given for construction and brick kiln workers and the need for widespread dissemination of information to workers about ways to protect themselves from extreme heat conditions through awareness camps, posters and banners at labour chowks etc. The ministry has also issued instructions to its organisations (DGLW, CLC, DTNBWED, VVGNLI, DGFASLI, DGMS, ESIC) to conduct awareness sessions and to include specific modules in their training programmes focusing on educating workers about causes and impact of heat wave, recognising heat stress, preventive strategies and ways to mitigate adverse effects of heatwave. Hospitals and dispensaries under DGLW and ESIC have also been asked to set up dedicated desks to take care of heat stroke cases and ensure adequate supply of ORS, ice packs and other heat illness prevention material. ***** Himanshu Pathak (Release ID: 2123477)

Heat and Pregnancy: Guidance for Healthcare Professionals and Community Health Workers How heat exposure impacts maternal and fetal health outcomes Extreme environmental heat exposure during pregnancy can lead to higher health risks for pregnant women and the fetus. High-intensity and prolonged heat exposure raises the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, while even a single extremely hot day can be harmful. Specific impacts documented from global and Indian research are as follows: Maternal health outcomes Extreme heat exposure increases the risk of severe maternal complications, mainly because of cardiovascular stress. This risk is high with long-term exposure during pregnancy (especially in the third trimester) and even higher with short-term exposure in the last week Heat exposure in early pregnancy (first 20 weeks) is linked to a higher risk of hypertensive disorders such as gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and gestational diabetes Maternal emergency visits and hospital admissions increase due to heat exposure, leading to a rise in all-cause maternal morbidity Seasonal variation shows that there are more cases of miscarriages during summer months, while pregnancies that begin in winter are linked to higher maternal morbidity Heat exposure leads to an increase in anxiety, psychological stress, sleep disturbance, fatigue, irritability, and contribute to perinatal depression Fetal outcomes Neonatal admissions and morbidity increase with heat exposure, with stronger evidence for admissions than for morbidity. Heat exposure at any stage of pregnancy increases the risk of preterm birth, and can also cause stillbirth, low birth weight, and congenital anomalies. Pregnancy outcomes • Work-related heat exposure (in ≥30 °C+ ≥35% humidity) in occupational or household settings combined with moderate to intense physical activity raises the risks related to pregnancy: The risk of miscarriage during the first trimester is three times higher. The risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes doubles. • Exposure to high heat and air pollution (due to high ozone, dust, particulate matter or wildfire) further increases the risks of adverse pregnancy outcomes, especially preterm birth. It is focused on a case study of the challenges faced and solutions deployed to combat increasing temperatures by self-employed women workers living within a specific informal settlement or slum in Ahmedabad, India. In this case, they are supported by a Non-Governmental Organisation (NGO) called Mahila Housing Trust (MHT). As per their website, the unique nature of MHT’s work is to improve urban built environments in poor communities through the collective action of poor, selfemployed women residents, x with an increasing focus on building climate resilience, in recent years. The research undertaken aims to shed light on the unique vulnerabilities faced by these women due to extreme heat and explores how MHT is actively supporting them to adapt to the heat impacts of the changing climate. This is a relatively new field of study as the disproportionate impacts of climate change, especially rising temperatures on poor, informal sector women workers and innovative adaptation measures to increase their resilience, are only now becoming more evident. This research case study is an attempt to add to the body of knowledge in this urgent, emerging area of study and suggest recommendations for the future. This highlighted the innovative climate resilience activities involving informal sector women workers ongoing in Ahmedabad, facilitated by MHT. xi Upon a written request, MHT allowed primary fieldwork to be undertaken in one of its partner informal urban settlements. The city of Ahmedabad is located in the state of Gujarat, in western India. Bordering the Thar Desert, it has limited vegetational cover due to it being a semi-arid state. The Indian Monsoons also provide little to no relief to the city. Currently it has an estimated population of 8.6 million xii with around 40% living in informal settlements or slums. xiii This city is an ideal location to assess the impacts of climate induced heating as it lies on the Tropic of Cancer. Therefore, it is constantly bearing the brunt of the latest impacts of global warming, throughout the year. However, the city feels it is perennially stuck in one season, that is the sweltering summer. A recent report by CEPT University and World Bank indicated that Ahmedabad gets a universal 4 thermal climate index (UTCI) above 46 points on 331 of 365 days- the highest for a South Asian city studied for the survey xiv. By 2035, it is projected that 11 million people will be at high risk of living inside an urban heat island within Ahmedabad and its surrounding areas. xv Why Bapalaal Kadiya ni Chaali MHT has been working since 2018 in partnership with Bapalaal Kadiya ni Chaali, an informal urban settlement which was established in 1940. Located in the north east of Ahmedabad, the settlement has a current estimated population of 800 with a total of 160 households.
